title: Race on the bandstand and on the road
summary: Ernie Watts and Charlie Owens could not swim in Florida; Elvin did not see color.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Through your career have there been times where there was any racial subject coming into play? Black and white musicians etcetera?

Yeah. That’s just understand — that goes on. At that time when that used to go on on Buddy’s band, not so much the members of the band but we would play Florida and Ernie Watts and Charlie Owens could not swim in the swimming pool, and this was, we’re talking about ’69, 70 you know. Elvin’s band was not so much amongst the band members, it was more or less sometimes people who assumed certain things in Europe, that the band was all black and then I show up. At certain times I was the only white guy on the band. But never amongst the players. Occasionally there was a few guys that came on with some attitudes. Listen, you know, what are you going to do? I mean I grew up in a town that had that when I was a kid. It’s as silly as we’re looking at is the lowest ebb at one point in the town that I grew up in, so it was a whole different thing. I mean I never felt it but it was just, that was going on. It never bothered me. And it never bothered

Elvin. Elvin didn’t see color. He was not — no never. We got off a train one time in Germany and the guy that booked us was this whole German Luftwaffe pilot who basically met us at the train. It was me, David Williams, who was from Trinidad; and Elvin; and Ryo Kawasaki was from Japan. And he comes up with a German accent and he says, “Well I thought you was an all-colored band?” He tells Elvin. And Elvin goes, “Well, we’re all colors,” he said.
That’s a good one. Well music is just like every other part of society you know, it’s everywhere.
